name: Modimelanotide

lead: Modimelanotide is a melanocortin peptide derived from alpha-MSH, the hormone behind skin and hair pigment.
It was developed for acute kidney injury rather than tanning, and development stopped after trials failed.

paras: It activates several melanocortin receptors (MC1, MC3, MC4, MC5). MC1 is the pigmentation receptor.
It is investigational and not an approved product, and its development was abandoned.

chain: MC1 activation is the pigmentation pathway
Skin and hair pigmentation in the alpha-MSH family
angle.text: Modimelanotide is an alpha-MSH analog, and MC1 activation by this family drives melanin production, the basis of pigmentation and tanning. Its own development targeted kidney injury, not tanning.

lead: Modimelanotide (AP-214, ABT-719, ZP-1480) is a synthetic peptide derived from alpha-MSH, the hormone that drives skin and hair pigmentation. It belongs to the melanocortin family alongside afamelanotide and Melanotan II, which people discuss for pigmentation and tanning, because it activates the MC1 receptor on pigment cells among others.[1][2][3]

It was developed by Action Pharma, Abbott, AbbVie and Zealand and studied for acute kidney injury, where it had shown efficacy in animal models but failed in clinical trials, so development stopped.[1] No pigmentation or tanning use of modimelanotide has been studied.[1]

paras: It is a non-selective melanocortin receptor agonist, with reported IC50 values of 2.9 nM at MC1, 1.9 nM at MC3, 3.7 nM at MC4 and 110 nM at MC5, making it most potent at MC3, closely followed by MC1 and MC4.[1] Alpha-MSH itself is a 13-amino-acid peptide cleaved from ACTH, and MC1 activation drives its pigmentation effect.[2]

In the wider melanocortin system, MC1R on melanocytes drives melanin production, MC3R and MC4R in the brain regulate energy balance (MC4R also sexual function), and MC5R is highly expressed in skin and adrenal glands. Afamelanotide, an MC1R agonist, is approved for erythropoietic protoporphyria, and bremelanotide was FDA approved in 2019 for hypoactive sexual desire disorder.[3]
The compound was studied for acute kidney injury, showing efficacy in animal models but failing in clinical trials.[1]
No studies found for appearance or pigmentation uses. Kidney injury trials are the only human studies reported, and they did not succeed.[1]
